The framework descriptor Shapley values demonstrated much greater variability compared with the adsorbate descriptors, as reflected in Figure 11. In particular, lsd_p can contribute between -0.07 and +0.07 (i.e., it can reduce or increase the fraction of entropy retained relative to gas phase by up to 7%), lsd_f can contribute between -0.15 and +0.06, density can contribute between -0.08 and +0.06, and ASA can contribute between -0.09 and +0.03. Among the framework features, lsd_f exhibits the strongest variation in Shapley values, suggesting that it is most influential in predicting the entropy ratio. These trends can be largely rationalized based on geometric arguments related to confinement. The negative trend with respect to the density feature can be explained by its inverse correlation with framework size. A larger density of sites in a zeolite usually corresponds to smaller pore sizes or reduced occupiable volume, which increases confinement and thereby reduces the fraction of retained entropy. We point the reader to Figure S11 for a heatmap of the feature correlation matrix. In contrast, the largest spherical diameter that can be included along a free path (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere (lsd_f) show positive trends between the Shapley value and their respective feature value. Large lsd_f or lsd_p values generally result in greater retention of entropy among the adsorbate due to the presence of large cages, bearing voids where the adsorbate retains translational and potentially rotational freedom. We emphasize that a small lsd_f or lsd_p does not exclusively guarantee a small entropy ratio; rather, a combination among the framework features is the best predictor. In particular, for frameworks with especially small lsd_f (<2 [Å]), we find that on average, more entropy is retained among the adsorbates than within larger lsd_f frameworks (consider Figure S12). This phenomenon suggests the presence of "ink bottle"-shaped pores, where the channels connecting the larger pores of the framework are smaller and entropically less favorable than the cages that precede them. The U-shaped trend within Figure 12M for small lsd_f (<2 [Å]) is therefore explained as small adsorbates exclusively fitting within small frameworks and consequently those systems exhibiting larger surviving entropies than their presence within larger lsd_f frameworks.

The framework descriptor Shapley values demonstrated much greater variability compared with the adsorbate descriptors, as reflected in Figure 11. In particular, lsd_p can contribute between -0.07 and +0.07 (i.e., it can reduce or increase the fraction of entropy retained relative to gas phase by up to 7%), lsd_f can contribute between -0.15 and +0.06, density can contribute between -0.08 and +0.06, and ASA can contribute between -0.09 and +0.03. Among the framework features, lsd_f exhibits the strongest variation in Shapley values, suggesting that it is most influential in predicting the entropy ratio. These trends can be largely rationalized based on geometric arguments related to confinement. The negative trend with respect to the density feature can be explained by its inverse correlation with framework size. A larger density of sites in a zeolite usually corresponds to smaller pore sizes or reduced occupiable volume, which increases confinement and thereby reduces the fraction of retained entropy. We point the reader to Figure S11 for a heatmap of the feature correlation matrix. In contrast, the largest spherical diameter that can be included along a free path (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere (lsd_f) show positive trends between the Shapley value and their respective feature value. Large lsd_f or lsd_p values generally result in greater retention of entropy among the adsorbate due to the presence of large cages, bearing voids where the adsorbate retains translational and potentially rotational freedom. We emphasize that a small lsd_f or lsd_p does not exclusively guarantee a small entropy ratio; rather, a combination among the framework features is the best predictor. In particular, for frameworks with especially small lsd_f (<2 [Å]), we find that on average, more entropy is retained among the adsorbates than within larger lsd_f frameworks (consider Figure S12). This phenomenon suggests the presence of "ink bottle"-shaped pores, where the channels connecting the larger pores of the framework are smaller and entropically less favorable than the cages that precede them. The U-shaped trend within Figure 12M for small lsd_f (<2 [Å]) is therefore explained as small adsorbates exclusively fitting within small frameworks and consequently those systems exhibiting larger surviving entropies than their presence within larger lsd_f frameworks.

items.quote: Nevertheless , linear relationships between the adsorbed and gas-phase entropies persist for acidic $ ^ { 25 } $ and siliceous frameworks , $ ^ { 10 } $ suggesting that geometric descriptors may be suitable in further developing empirical correlations . The ideal gas entropy can be rigorously derived using statistical mechanics and depends on the degrees of freedom of the molecule. The greatest contributions to the gas-phase entropy are typically from the translational and rotational modes, which under isothermal conditions primarily depend on the system volume and principle moments of inertia of the molecule, respectively. Considering that adsorption limits the accessible volume and potentially hinders the rotational freedom of a molecule, it is conceivable that the entropy of adsorption may be predicted by using geometric arguments. For example, Denayer et al. have demonstrated that the driving force behind the zeolitic separation of alkane/isoalkane mixtures is exclusively the difference in rotational loss, represented by a ratio between the molecule's radius of gyration and the cavity's largest inscribed van der Waals radius. $ ^{26} $ De Moor et al. $ ^{27} $ used ab initio simulations to show that the adsorption entropies for n-alkanes within acidic zeolites are linearly correlated with their carbon number. Janda et al. $ ^{28} $ have studied the topological effects of protonic zeolites on the thermodynamics of n-alkane adsorption using Monte Carlo simulations. The conclusions of their work showed that for unidimensional zeolites without cages, the ratio of the minimum to maximum channel diameters positively correlate with the entropy and enthalpy of adsorption. In particular, the enthalpy and entropy of adsorption become less negative for adsorption within channels which are oval shaped and are most negative for circular-shaped channels. They showed that the presence/absence of framework cages also impacts the thermodynamics of adsorption, suggesting that the alkanes exhibit more rotational freedom in cages vs channels. Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman $ ^{25} $ compiled experimentally determined adsorption entropies for alkanes adsorbed in nine aluminosilicate zeolites. They showed that the entropic loss upon adsorption could be linearly correlated with the molecule's gas-phase translational and rotational entropies and that the occupiable volume of a zeolite is a “universal” descriptor in predicting such losses. In a separate study, $ ^{10} $ we have qualitatively reproduced the trends found in Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman's work for a larger set of molecules within pure-silica zeolites using Monte Carlo calculations of the adsorption entropy at infinitely dilute conditions. In general, these works suggest that the adsorbate characteristics are relatively unimportant and support the perception that models based primarily on adsorbent characteristics may be an effective tool trends found in Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman ' s work for a larger set of molecules within pure-silica zeolites using Monte Carlo calculations of the adsorption entropy at infinitely dilute conditions . In general , these works suggest that the adsorbate characteristics are relatively unimportant and support the perception that models based primarily on adsorbent characteristics may be an effective tool in predicting the entropy of adsorption and other thermodynamic adsorption quantities.

The linear trend lines in Figure 1 yield the following slopes: FAU: 0.86, LTA: 0.87, MOR: 0.84, MFI: 0.76, and FER: 0.74. The framework descriptor Shapley values demonstrated much greater variability compared with the adsorbate descriptors, as reflected in Figure 11. In particular, lsd_p can contribute between -0.07 and +0.07 (i.e., it can reduce or increase the fraction of entropy retained relative to gas phase by up to 7%), lsd_f can contribute between -0.15 and +0.06, density can contribute between -0.08 and +0.06, and ASA can contribute between -0.09 and +0.03. Among the framework features, lsd_f exhibits the strongest variation in Shapley values, suggesting that it is most influential in predicting the entropy ratio. These trends can be largely rationalized based on geometric arguments related to confinement. The negative trend with respect to the density feature can be explained by its inverse correlation with framework size. A larger density of sites in a zeolite usually corresponds to smaller pore sizes or reduced occupiable volume, which increases confinement and thereby reduces the fraction of retained entropy. We point the reader to Figure S11 for a heatmap of the feature correlation matrix. In contrast, the largest spherical diameter that can be included along a free path (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere (lsd_f) show positive trends between the Shapley value and their respective feature value. Large lsd_f or lsd_p values generally result in greater retention of entropy among the adsorbate due to the presence of large cages, bearing voids where the adsorbate retains translational and potentially rotational freedom. We emphasize that a small lsd_f or lsd_p does not exclusively guarantee a small entropy ratio; rather, a combination among the framework features is the best predictor. In particular, for frameworks with especially small lsd_f (<2 [Å]), we find that on average, more entropy is retained among the adsorbates than within larger lsd_f frameworks (consider Figure S12). This phenomenon suggests the presence of "ink bottle"-shaped pores, where the channels connecting the larger pores of the framework are smaller and entropically less favorable than the cages that precede them. The U-shaped trend within Figure 12M for small lsd_f (<2 [Å]) is therefore explained as small adsorbates exclusively fitting within small frameworks and consequently those systems exhibiting larger surviving entropies than their presence within larger lsd_f frameworks.

items.quote: Nevertheless , linear relationships between the adsorbed and gas-phase entropies persist for acidic $ ^ { 25 } $ and siliceous frameworks , $ ^ { 10 } $ suggesting that geometric descriptors may be suitable in further developing empirical correlations . The ideal gas entropy can be rigorously derived using statistical mechanics and depends on the degrees of freedom of the molecule. The greatest contributions to the gas-phase entropy are typically from the translational and rotational modes, which under isothermal conditions primarily depend on the system volume and principle moments of inertia of the molecule, respectively. Considering that adsorption limits the accessible volume and potentially hinders the rotational freedom of a molecule, it is conceivable that the entropy of adsorption may be predicted by using geometric arguments. For example, Denayer et al. have demonstrated that the driving force behind the zeolitic separation of alkane/isoalkane mixtures is exclusively the difference in rotational loss, represented by a ratio between the molecule's radius of gyration and the cavity's largest inscribed van der Waals radius. $ ^{26} $ De Moor et al. $ ^{27} $ used ab initio simulations to show that the adsorption entropies for n-alkanes within acidic zeolites are linearly correlated with their carbon number. Janda et al. $ ^{28} $ have studied the topological effects of protonic zeolites on the thermodynamics of n-alkane adsorption using Monte Carlo simulations. The conclusions of their work showed that for unidimensional zeolites without cages, the ratio of the minimum to maximum channel diameters positively correlate with the entropy and enthalpy of adsorption. In particular, the enthalpy and entropy of adsorption become less negative for adsorption within channels which are oval shaped and are most negative for circular-shaped channels. They showed that the presence/absence of framework cages also impacts the thermodynamics of adsorption, suggesting that the alkanes exhibit more rotational freedom in cages vs channels. Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman $ ^{25} $ compiled experimentally determined adsorption entropies for alkanes adsorbed in nine aluminosilicate zeolites. They showed that the entropic loss upon adsorption could be linearly correlated with the molecule's gas-phase translational and rotational entropies and that the occupiable volume of a zeolite is a “universal” descriptor in predicting such losses. In a separate study, $ ^{10} $ we have qualitatively reproduced the trends found in Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman's work for a larger set of molecules within pure-silica zeolites using Monte Carlo calculations of the adsorption entropy at infinitely dilute conditions. In general, these works suggest that the adsorbate characteristics are relatively unimportant and support the perception that models based primarily on adsorbent characteristics may be an effective tool trends found in Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman ' s work for a larger set of molecules within pure-silica zeolites using Monte Carlo calculations of the adsorption entropy at infinitely dilute conditions . In general , these works suggest that the adsorbate characteristics are relatively unimportant and support the perception that models based primarily on adsorbent characteristics may be an effective tool in predicting the entropy of adsorption and other thermodynamic adsorption quantities.

This decrease in entropy upon transition state formation is likely caused by the loss of frustrated rotational and quasi-translational degrees of freedom present in noncovalently adsorbed species confined within zeolite catalysts . $ ^ { 50 , 109 } $ The apparent enthalpic activation barrier $(\Delta H_{\mathrm{app}})$ is about 7 kJ mol$^{-1}$ smaller on Sn-Beta-F than Sn-Beta-OH (Table 2), while both catalysts exhibit a similar entropy of activation ($~\sim$148 J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$). These differences in activation parameters reflect apparent activation free energy barriers that are $\sim$7 kJ mol$^{-1}$ (evaluated at 373 K) lower on Sn-Beta-F than on Sn-Beta-OH, which give rise to zero-order rate constants that are $\sim$10× larger on Sn-Beta-F(302) than on Sn-Beta-OH(326) (Figure 3). The lower apparent activation barriers on Sn-Beta-F(302) are likely due to the preferential enthalpic stabilization of the hydride-shift transition state, relative to the coadsorbed 2-butanol-cyclohexanone adduct, by the more tightly ordered intraporous solvent structure present in Sn-Beta-F (Figure 5) as the MPVO reaction is catalyzed by open Sn sites confined within pores of the same size in both Sn-Beta zeolites.

items.quote: Although the mass of the TraPPE-model molecules does not change , the symmetry number and principal moments of inertia within the rotational entropy equation are different . The linear trend lines in Figure 1 yield the following slopes: FAU: 0.86, LTA: 0.87, MOR: 0.84, MFI: 0.76, and FER: 0.74. The slopes appear to be related to zeolite size as this sequence of decreasing slope corresponds to the sequence of decreasing pore size. Further discussion on this point is reserved for later in this paper (cf. Section 4.2). We immediately point out that all of these slopes are larger than the proposed two-third based on adsorption to a flat surface. Given that the x-axis is the total entropy, not just translational and rotational contributions, we should not expect a precise slope of two-third. These slopes are, additionally, larger than the slopes for linear trend lines computed from the data of Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman (not present in their paper, but easily obtained using data in the Supporting Information of ref 13): FAU: 0.80, MOR: 0.75, MFI: 0.65, and FER: 0.59 (and other topologies not studied here). As a specific example, Figure 2 reproduces the entropy correlation for MFI (same as Figure 1) but includes the data from ref 13 for the same material; the slope based on Figure 2. Comparison of the linear correlation of adsorbed- and gas-phase entropies for MFI adsorbent, from the present simulation/model-based results (at 300 K) and the experimental calculations (at various temperatures) from Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman. $ ^{13} $ As noted in the figure, the slopes of the linear trend lines are 0.76 and 0.65 for the simulation and experimental data sets, respectively. The simulation/model results are for the diverse set of adsorbates studied here, whereas the experimental results are for alkanes of up to eight carbons, with propane as the smallest adsorbate (and the corresponding smallest $ s_{gas}^{0} $). We note that the model-based entropies are offset compared to the experiment due to the pseudo-atom structure of TraPPE molecules mentioned in the text.
